title: A hope with an address
hookLine: "when X happens, I will do Y" plans had medium-to-large effects in a review of the research (Gollwitzer and Sheeran)
carry: a when-then plan decides ahead of time

cards: "I'll meditate more." It's said on New Year's Eve, on Sunday nights, after a good retreat. It's sincere, and by Wednesday it has quietly evaporated.
Now try a different sentence: "When I set my coffee cup down after breakfast, then I'll sit for two minutes." Same hope, different shape. The first sentence is a wish floating in the air.
The second has an address and a time of arrival. Psychologists have a name for that second kind of sentence, and they have measured what the shape does. Today's word is the small hinge it turns on.

teach.b: First, the shape. Psychologist Peter Gollwitzer called these plans implementation intentions: when this situation arrives, then I will do that. A goal says what.
An implementation intention says when, where and how. Second, why it works.
The plan hands the decision to the moment ahead of time, so when the situation shows up, there's nothing left to decide.
The cue from earlier this week is back at work: the when becomes the cue, and the then becomes the routine. Third, the measurement.

Gollwitzer and Paschal Sheeran gathered the studies of these plans into one review, and found the effect on whether people followed through was medium to large, by the usual yardstick researchers use.
For one sentence, that's a real effect. Fourth, an old shape. Some traditions tied practice to set moments of the day long before the research.

teach.h: EVENING, AND MORNING, AND AT NOON.
teach.b: In the Psalms, the King James Bible has the line: "Evening, and morning, and at noon, will I pray, and cry aloud: and he shall hear my voice." Not "more often." Three appointments, each with a when.

And it ties this week together: ten minutes on the breath, attention trainable, almost half a day on habit, the cue, the place that holds it, less friction. Today's hinge is a when, a where, a small then.
That's how a hope becomes something that happens on an ordinary day.

how: People who want a practice to stick sometimes write it as a when-then plan, tying it to a moment that already happens each day; some religious traditions also set prayer or practice at fixed times of day.

o: the deadline for finishing a goal you have set
the hour of the day your willpower is at its peak
the moment that triggers a plan made ahead of time

games.q: you want to read one page of a book you love each day. which plan do you make?
o: "when I get into bed, then I'll read one page."
games.why: a when and a then. the research found plans shaped like this helped people follow through.

practice: Settle on the breath, then think of a moment that already happens every day, setting down your keys, the kettle clicking off, the engine going quiet: that's your when.

Choose a small then, three breaths, a minute of sitting, one line you value read slowly, and say the whole sentence silently once: "When this, then that." Picture the moment arriving and you doing it, then let it go and rest.

wordCard.voice: When. The first half of a when-then plan, which ties a small practice to a moment that already happens. Today's word.
